blocks.text: The anions (acid radicals) are identified by the following tests on the solid sample, each with its experiment, observation and inference.

Take about 2 g of the solid carbonate sample in a clean test tube and add about 5 cm3 of dilute HCl; pass the gas evolved through lime water. Effervescence takes place, a gas evolves briskly and it turns lime water milky: carbonate ions are indicated.

blocks.title: Carbonate test
blocks.text: CO3 2-(aq) + 2H+(aq) -> H2O(l) + CO2(g); Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) (white ppt) + H2O(l)
b) Chloride, bromide and iodide, Cl-, Br-, I-

Take 2 g of the solid sample in a test tube and add 5 cm3 of distilled water to make the aqueous solution. Add a few drops of dilute HNO3 to acidify the solution, then about 5 cm3 of aqueous AgNO3. A thick white precipitate that dissolves in aqueous NH3 indicates Cl-; a thick cream-yellow precipitate indicates Br-; a bright yellow precipitate indicates I- (Figure 16.7). The dilute nitric acid is added to prevent the precipitation of carbonate ions along with the halide ions.

blocks.title: Silver halides
blocks.text: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s) white ppt; Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq) -> AgBr(s) cream-yellow ppt; Ag+(aq) + I-(aq) -> AgI(s) bright yellow ppt

Take 2 g of the solid sample in a clean test tube and dissolve it in 5 cm3 of distilled water. Add 5 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution, then 3 g of powdered aluminium metal. A characteristic smell of ammonia gas is felt near the mouth of the test tube and the gas turns red litmus paper blue: nitrate ions are indicated. Aluminium metal reduces nitrate ions to ammonium ions, which react with the aqueous NaOH to evolve ammonia; the reduction of nitrate by aluminium is a redox reaction in which the aluminium acts as the reducing agent.

Take 3 g of the solid sample in a clean test tube and dissolve it in 5 cm3 of distilled water. Acidify the solution with a few drops of dilute HNO3 and add 5 cm3 of barium nitrate solution. A heavy white precipitate of BaSO4 is formed: sulfate ions are indicated. The dilute nitric acid destroys any carbonate ions present as an impurity.

blocks.alt: Top: a table of the anion tests with the ion, the reagent, the observation and the reaction for carbonate, the halides, nitrate and sulfate, with three circles for the white, cream and yellow silver halides. Bottom: a table of the cation tests with sodium hydroxide and with aqueous ammonia for Al3+, NH4+, Ca2+, Cr3+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+ and Zn2+, with the hydroxide equations and colour swatches.
blocks.caption: Identifying anions and cations in salt analysis (original diagram after topics 16.6 and 16.7 and Figure 16.7).
blocks.long_description: Carbonate gives brisk effervescence with dilute hydrochloric acid and the gas turns lime water milky. Halides, after acidifying with dilute nitric acid to remove carbonate, give silver precipitates: white and soluble in ammonia for chloride, cream-yellow for bromide, bright yellow for iodide. Nitrate warmed with sodium hydroxide and aluminium powder gives ammonia, which turns red litmus blue, and sulfate gives a heavy white precipitate with barium nitrate. Among the cations, sodium hydroxide gives a white gelatinous precipitate with aluminium, ammonia gas with ammonium, white precipitates with calcium (insoluble in excess) and zinc (soluble in excess), green with chromium (dissolving in excess) and iron(II) (turning orange-brown), light blue with copper and orange-brown with iron(III); aqueous ammonia then distinguishes them, giving almost nothing with calcium, a deep blue solution with copper, and redissolving the zinc precipitate.

blocks.text: Distinguish carbonate from bicarbonate, describe the ring test for nitrate, and name some water-insoluble sulfates.
